title: Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue within Accessibility, Security, and User Experience. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: A frontend can guide a user but cannot make authorization, inventory, payments, or access-control decisions authoritative by itself.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue: Accessible interaction design
content_blocks.alt_text: Accessible interaction design diagram for lesson 124: Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue. Use meaningful elements, names, and labels → Preserve focus and expected navigation → Announce errors and updates in text
content_blocks.caption: Accessibility workflow: make controls understandable, keyboard-operable, and clear when dynamic status changes.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Accessible and secure Vue interfaces use semantic HTML, labels, keyboard support, safe rendering, and explicit backend trust boundaries. This lesson focuses on Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Semantic HTML
items.text: For Semantic HTML, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Accessible names and labels
items.text: For Accessible names and labels, use semantic HTML first, ensure controls have accessible names, preserve visible keyboard focus, communicate errors in text, and verify that updates remain understandable without color or animation alone.

items.title: Keyboard navigation
items.text: For Keyboard navigation, use semantic HTML first, ensure controls have accessible names, preserve visible keyboard focus, communicate errors in text, and verify that updates remain understandable without color or animation alone.

items.title: Focus management
items.text: For Focus management, use semantic HTML first, ensure controls have accessible names, preserve visible keyboard focus, communicate errors in text, and verify that updates remain understandable without color or animation alone.

items.title: Accessible interactive controls
items.text: For Accessible interactive controls, use semantic HTML first, ensure controls have accessible names, preserve visible keyboard focus, communicate errors in text, and verify that updates remain understandable without color or animation alone.

content_blocks.expected_output: The input has an accessible label and hint; the status region can announce important asynchronous updates.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run as App.vue and test with keyboard only. For live announcements, update the status text only when a meaningful state change occurs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Accessible names and labels”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Accessible and secure Vue interfaces use semantic HTML, labels, keyboard support, safe rendering, and explicit backend trust boundaries. For Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue” that applies “Semantic HTML”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Semantic HTML”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Accessibility Fundamentals in Vue belongs to the broader area Accessibility, Security, and User Experience.
The main concept to practice is Semantic HTML.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
